Negative Marking: Penalty Fractions, Wrong Answers and Blanks

Translate a negative-marking rule into raw marks, distinguish a fraction of a mark from a fraction of the reward, and compare practice tests fairly.

By GradeTargetCalc · Published 2 November 2026 · 5 min read

In this guide
Identify exactly what the penalty is measured againstConvert a fractional penalty into marks per wrong answerWorked example: compare attempted accuracy with net marksA blank and a wrong answer can have different effectsCompare practice sessions with a consistent scoring ruleSeparate an illustrative rule from an official reported scoreRecord the complete rule before calculatingFAQsSources
01

Identify exactly what the penalty is measured against

Negative marking means incorrect answers deduct marks under a stated scoring rule. But phrases such as a quarter penalty are incomplete without units. A deduction of 0.25 marks is different from deducting one quarter of the reward for a correct answer when that reward is four marks.

Start with the current instructions for the exact examination and section. Do not transfer a familiar practice-test rule to another assessment. Some tests deduct marks for incorrect answers, others do not, and raw marks may later be transformed. The negative-marking calculator is a configurable arithmetic model; it does not identify an exam’s current policy from its name.

02

Convert a fractional penalty into marks per wrong answer

Suppose a hypothetical test awards four marks per correct answer and deducts one quarter of that reward for a wrong answer. The deduction is four × 0.25 = one mark. Enter 1 as the positive penalty amount; the calculator subtracts it automatically.

If the instructions instead deduct a flat quarter mark, enter 0.25. On ten incorrect answers, these rules deduct ten marks and 2.5 marks respectively. The difference is substantial despite the similar wording. Write the reward and the deduction in the same marks-per-question units before entering either value.

03

Worked example: compare attempted accuracy with net marks

Consider 50 equally valued questions, four marks for correct answers, one mark deducted for wrong answers and zero for blanks. A practice tally of 32 correct, ten incorrect and eight blank earns 32 × 4 − 10 × 1 = 118 raw marks. The maximum is 50 × 4 = 200, so the raw percentage is 59%.

Attempted-question accuracy is a different measure: 32 correct out of 42 attempted is approximately 76.19%. Correct answers as a share of all questions is 64%. Neither figure is the 59% net mark percentage. Keeping the labels separate prevents a practice dashboard’s accuracy number from being mistaken for the awarded examination score.

04

A blank and a wrong answer can have different effects

Under this hypothetical rule, replacing one wrong answer with a blank raises the score by one mark because the deduction disappears. Replacing one wrong answer with a correct answer raises the score by five marks: a one-mark loss becomes a four-mark reward. Those are descriptions of outcomes after answers are known.

They are not a universal instruction to leave uncertain questions blank. During an examination, the eventual correctness of an uncertain answer is unknown. Appropriate choices depend on the official instructions, time available and the uncertainty attached to that particular question. A completed tally cannot establish the best strategy for every future question.

05

Compare practice sessions with a consistent scoring rule

Suppose another session has 30 correct, four wrong and 16 blank under the same 50-question rule. Its raw score is 120 − 4 = 116 marks, or 58%. Attempted accuracy is 30 ÷ 34 × 100, approximately 88.24%, higher than the first session, yet its net score is slightly lower.

This does not make accuracy useless. It shows that attempted accuracy alone misses the number of rewarded answers and deducted marks. Keep correct, incorrect, blank, total questions, reward and penalty alongside each practice result. If test lengths or scoring rules differ, recompute comparable measures instead of ranking sessions by one unlabeled percentage.

06

Separate an illustrative rule from an official reported score

An official provider’s instructions illustrate why assumptions must be checked. ETS states that the GRE General Test’s Verbal Reasoning and Quantitative Reasoning measures do not subtract marks for incorrect answers. A negative-marking strategy copied from another test would therefore be inappropriate for those stated measures.

A historical NTA JEE Main 2022 instruction document, by contrast, describes specified sections with four marks for correct answers, a one-mark deduction and zero for unanswered items. That source is a historical example, not verification of the current rules for a future examination. Always read the latest applicable instructions before entering a scoring model.

07

Record the complete rule before calculating

The calculator accepts a positive wrong-answer penalty and subtracts it from the reward total. Its raw result can be negative; it does not silently apply a zero floor, curve or official score conversion. If your examination does apply those adjustments, the raw calculation is only an intermediate step.

  • Confirm reward and deduction in marks per question.
  • Check how blanks, multiple selections and disputed questions are treated.
  • Keep separate records for sections with different question values.
  • Label raw marks, net percentage and attempted accuracy separately.
Quick answers

Frequently asked questions

Should the penalty input have a minus sign?

No. Enter the positive amount deducted per wrong answer. The calculator subtracts it; entering a negative amount would misstate the model.

Is attempted accuracy the same as raw percentage?

No. Attempted accuracy excludes blanks and ignores the scoring reward and deduction. Net percentage uses awarded marks divided by the full available maximum.

Does this predict a standardized exam score?

No. Scaling, section rules and official reporting conversions require the provider’s actual method. A configurable raw-mark example is not an official scaled-score prediction.
